title: What are BiConsumer<T,U>, BiPredicate<T,U>, and BiFunction<T,U,R>, when do you use these two-argument functional interfaces (e.g. Map.forEach, Map.merge, Map.compute), and how do they relate to their single-argument counterparts?
keyPoints: BiConsumer takes two inputs and returns void: used by Map.forEach(key, value -> action)
BiFunction takes two inputs and returns a result: used by Map.merge, Map.compute, and Map.replaceAll
BiPredicate takes two inputs and returns boolean: used for conditions that need two arguments
The Bi prefix adds one more parameter to the single-argument counterpart
All compose with andThen (BiConsumer, BiFunction) or and/or/negate (BiPredicate)
For three or more arguments there are no built-in TriFunction/TriConsumer: use custom functional interfaces
Map operations are the primary use case for Bi variants in production code

s1_definition.oneliner: BiConsumer, BiPredicate, and BiFunction are two-argument versions of the core functional interfaces, used primarily with Map operations like forEach, merge, and compute.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **BiConsumer<T,U>** – `(T, U) -> void`; used by `Map.forEach(key, value -> action)`.
- **BiFunction<T,U,R>** – `(T, U) -> R`; used by `Map.merge`, `Map.compute`, `Map.replaceAll`.
- **BiPredicate<T,U>** – `(T, U) -> boolean`; used for two-input conditions, composable with `and()`, `or()`, `negate()`.
- **Relationship** – "Bi" adds one more parameter: Consumer(T->void) becomes BiConsumer(T,U->void).
- **No TriFunction** – for three or more arguments, define a custom `@FunctionalInterface`.
s1_definition.analogy: Consumer takes one thing and acts on it (process one cheque). BiConsumer takes two things (process a key-value pair: account number and balance). Map.forEach gives you both the key and the value, so you need BiConsumer to accept both.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Bi-variant Relationships:

  Consumer<T>         ──+1 param──▶  BiConsumer<T, U>
  T -> void                          (T, U) -> void
  list.forEach            Map.forEach

  Function<T, R>      ──+1 param──▶  BiFunction<T, U, R>
  T -> R                             (T, U) -> R
  stream.map              Map.merge, Map.compute

  Predicate<T>        ──+1 param──▶  BiPredicate<T, U>
  T -> boolean                       (T, U) -> boolean
  stream.filter           two-input conditions
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
BiConsumer, BiPredicate, and BiFunction are two-argument versions of the core functional interfaces. BiConsumer takes two inputs and returns void, used by `Map.forEach`. BiFunction takes two inputs and returns a result, used by `Map.merge`, `Map.compute`, and `Map.replaceAll`. BiPredicate takes two inputs and returns boolean.

The relationship is simple: Bi adds one more parameter. Consumer becomes BiConsumer, Function becomes BiFunction, Predicate becomes BiPredicate. For three or more arguments, there are no built-in variants; define a custom `@FunctionalInterface`.

In banking, `Map.merge("RELIANCE", amount, BigDecimal::add)` uses BiFunction to sum duplicate trades. `Map.forEach((accountId, balance) -> log)` uses BiConsumer. `Map.replaceAll((id, bal) -> bal.multiply(rate))` applies interest to all balances.

Remember one sentence: BiConsumer, BiPredicate, and BiFunction are the two-argument versions of Consumer, Predicate, and Function, used primarily with Map operations.
